orders.explanation: Transcript 1 shows stronger adaptability and problem-solving under constraints: when common Python tooling and packages were unavailable, it implemented structure learning (BIC-scored linear-Gaussian regression), intervention (edge cutting into Y), and sampling using only the standard library, and still produced all required artifacts. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds but spends substantial time on avoidable API/usage errors (pgmpy import changes, estimator signatures, memory blow-up with EM, simulate kwargs), relying heavily on trial-and-error with external libraries and system package installation. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates more robust, self-sufficient capability.

Transcript 2 shows stronger adaptability and technical depth: after discovering that standard scientific Python libraries weren’t available, it implemented structure learning (linear-Gaussian BIC scoring, acyclicity checks) and parameter fitting/sampling entirely from scratch, while enforcing the given constraints and intervention semantics. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but spends substantial effort wrestling with package installation and shifting pgmpy APIs, with multiple dead ends and errors before converging. The ability to robustly complete the task under constrained tooling indicates higher capability in Transcript 2.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it correctly infers the full transformation, iteratively debugs why the initial macro approach hangs (discovering that `:%s` inside a `:%normal!`-executed macro causes problems), and converges on a simpler, faster set of macros. It thoroughly validates correctness on increasing file sizes up to the full 1M lines and confirms byte-for-byte equality with `diff`/`md5sum`. Transcript 1 never resolves the whitespace issue, fails its own full-file comparison, and ends by asserting success without actually achieving a match.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it systematically diagnosed the transformation, iteratively debugged why the initial macro approach hung under `-Es`, and empirically validated performance and correctness up to the full 1M-row file with `diff`/hash checks. It also identified and fixed subtle issues (e.g., `%` range behavior inside a macro under Ex mode and regex efficiency) and produced a final script proven to match expected output byte-for-byte. Transcript 2 never achieves a clean full-file validation (its intermediate diffs remain wrong due to already-modified input) and ends with an unverified “should match” claim based only on a one-line test.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it inspects the provided code, correctly reasons about the cost model, iteratively tunes both the global shape set and gen_len-aware batching, and actually writes/validates final plan files while checking the global MAX_SHAPES constraint across buckets. Transcript 2 contains substantial confusion about what drives padding/cost, multiple contradictory conclusions (including briefly claiming the task was impossible), and ends mid-verification with incomplete output code, suggesting weaker reliability and execution discipline despite eventually converging on a workable configuration.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper and more accurate understanding of the provided cost model, including the key (non-obvious) insight that `pad_prefill` and batch compute cost depend on `align(prompt_len, 64)` and per-batch `S_max/G_max`, not on the declared `shape.seq_align` (except for compilation cost). It then uses that insight to run structured ablations over shape-sets and per-shape batch sizing, converging on a configuration that satisfies all constraints. Transcript 2 reaches a valid solution as well, but its approach is more heuristic/parameter-tweaking, includes some avoidable tooling errors, and shows less principled linkage between the cost model’s mechanics and the final design choices.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it correctly verifies bundle refs, fetches both bundles into the required local branches, performs an actual `git merge branch2` into `branch1`, resolves the merge conflict in `algo.py`, and produces a real merge commit with two parents. It then implements a simple, clearly-justified `map` function matching the examples and validates it end-to-end. Transcript 1 mishandles the merge (it fails due to local changes and then commits without completing a merge, even deleting files), making the repository state inconsistent with the task requirement to merge branch2 into branch1.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly fetches both bundles into `branch1` and `branch2`, performs an actual merge (producing a true merge commit with two parents), resolves the `algo.py` conflict, and verifies the solution against all examples. Transcript 2’s merge step fails (“local changes would be overwritten by merge; strategy ort failed”) and then it commits anyway, meaning `branch2` was not truly merged into `branch1` despite the transcript claiming completion. Transcript 1 also derives and implements the simplest correct generalization directly from the examples, whereas Transcript 2’s solution is more complex but built atop an incorrect git state.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it executes the task cleanly end-to-end with correct OpenSSL usage, sensible file permissions (including protecting the combined PEM), and a robust Python verification script that reliably extracts CN and expiration date. Transcript 2 shows repeated trial-and-error (missing dependencies, incorrect API usage, broken CN parsing) and leaves insecure permissions (e.g., `server.pem` world-readable and `/app/ssl` at default 755), which violates the “ensure correct permissions” requirement.

Transcript 2 shows stronger execution quality: it follows a clear plan, uses robust OpenSSL commands (including `-sha256`), sets appropriate permissions (notably `600` on the combined PEM since it contains the private key), and creates a Python script that works on a minimal environment without third‑party dependencies. Transcript 1 is significantly less reliable, with multiple failed iterations (missing `cryptography`, incorrect `ssl` API usage, repeated CN parsing bugs) before arriving at a working script, indicating weaker debugging and implementation discipline.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it delivers a more robust final program in both languages: it includes proper argument-count checks, input validation, and clearer error handling, and it avoids undefined behavior in C when the argument is missing or invalid. Transcript 2 eventually finds a simpler polyglot structure, but its final code is comparatively brittle (e.g., no `argc` check and `atol` without validation), and much of the transcript is prolonged trial-and-error without improving robustness.

Transcript 2 is produced by the more capable model because it converges on a correct, robust polyglot structure with clearer separation of C vs Python parsing, and it adds proper argument validation/error messages in both languages. Transcript 1 eventually finds a working trick, but it shows extensive flailing, multiple incorrect polyglot attempts, and ends with weaker input handling (e.g., no argc checks and naive `atol`). Overall, Transcript 2 demonstrates better engineering judgment and code quality despite an initially flawed attempt.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it produces a fully generic, content-preserving resharding scheme that works for arbitrary files (not just JSONL), enforces both constraints at every directory level via a fixed-depth base‑30 chunk tree, and includes robust metadata (permissions/mtime) with verified round‑trip hashing. It also detects and fixes a real constraint violation during testing, demonstrating stronger debugging and systems thinking. Transcript 2 is narrower (line-based JSONL concatenation), has brittle assumptions, higher memory use, and a shakier uv/pyproject setup path before arriving at a workable state.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it designs a truly generic, scalable resharding format: it chunks arbitrary binary files by size (≤15MB), stores a precise manifest including permissions/mtimes, and uses a fixed-depth base-30 directory tree to guarantee the ≤30-entries-per-directory invariant at every level. It also demonstrates stronger engineering rigor by detecting a constraint violation in testing, revising the design to fix it, and then re-testing with programmatic validation and hash-based round-trip verification. Transcript 1 eventually works on the sample but relies on loading all lines into memory and concatenating JSONL content, which is less robust and less general for other datasets/sizes.

Transcript 1 is markedly more capable: it efficiently inspects the ontology, correctly identifies the relevant predicates, and produces a clean SPARQL 1.1 query that properly enforces (a) full-professor status, (b) at least one EU-country workplace, and (c) existence of a department with >10 currently enrolled students via a well-formed aggregated subquery inside `FILTER EXISTS`. Transcript 2 shows substantial confusion about SPARQL syntax and query structuring (repeatedly proposing invalid constructs like non-standard `INCLUDE`, `WITH/AS`, and `FROM { ... }`), only converging very late after many incorrect rewrites—indicating weaker mastery and reliability despite ending with a plausible approach.

Transcript 2 is produced by the more capable model because it efficiently identifies the relevant ontology terms, cleanly encodes both “EU country” and “>10 currently enrolled students” constraints using standard SPARQL 1.1 constructs (VALUES, FILTER EXISTS, and an aggregated subquery), and writes a coherent final query without repeated incorrect rewrites. Transcript 1 shows extensive confusion about SPARQL subquery legality and repeatedly generates invalid/unfinished queries before eventually landing on something plausible, indicating weaker command of SPARQL and query structuring.
